description.text: Jonah was a Jewish prophet from Gath‑hepher in the Northern Kingdom of Israel around the 8th century BCE. He is the central figure of the Book of Jonah, a minor prophetic book that records his reluctance to deliver God’s judgment to the city of Nineveh, his attempt to flee to Jaffa, his being cast overboard, swallowed by a large fish, surviving three days and nights, and finally being released to complete his mission.

The narrative of Jonah has been interpreted across Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. In Judaism it is read on Yom Kippur as a lesson in repentance; in Christianity Jesus refers to Jonah’s three‑day stay in the fish as a sign of his own resurrection; in Islam Jonah (Yūnus) is a prophet and the Quran contains a chapter named after him. Scholars debate the historicity of the story, with some suggesting it is satirical or allegorical and noting that the Hebrew text simply calls the creature a “great fish” rather than a whale.

curiosities.text: The Hebrew text refers to the creature that swallowed Jonah as a “great fish” (dag gadol), not a whale, and the term has been the subject of speculation by naturalists in the 17th and 18th centuries.
In the New Testament Jesus cites Jonah’s three days in the fish as a foreshadowing of his own resurrection, calling it the “sign of Jonah.”
Jonah is the only one of the Twelve Minor Prophets to be named in the Quran, and the tenth chapter of the Quran is called Surah Yūnus after him.
Some modern Bible scholars suggest that the Book of Jonah is fictional and satirical, composed long after the events it describes, based on postexilic Aramaic language and motifs.
